intro: The finale begins with a violin melody that neither violin section plays complete: the notes pass between them. After the preceding march’s G-major finish, this slow lament takes the symphony back to B minor and leaves it there.

cues.title: One tune, two violin sections
cues.text: The first and second violins exchange notes of a falling melody. Neither section has the whole tune on its page; together they make one continuous lament. The first chord already aches, a half-diminished chord in the symphony’s B-minor home.
cues.evidence: Queensland Symphony Orchestra, Symphony No. 6 learning resource, p. 16, reproduces the divided melody. Opening harmony: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphony_No._6_(Tchaikovsky). https://qso.com.au/uploads/QSO-Learning-Resource-Breathtaking-Tchaikovsky-1-.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The ending comes first
cues.text: On 23 February 1893, months before the orchestration, Tchaikovsky tells Vladimir Davydov that the finale will be “a long drawn-out adagio”. In the same letter he writes of feeling blissfully sure that he can still compose.
cues.evidence: Tchaikovsky to Vladimir Davydov, letter 4865, 11/23 February 1893. https://en.tchaikovsky-research.net/pages/Symphony_No._6

cues.title: D major, still falling
cues.text: Horns support a broad new melody in the first violins and violas. It is in D major, and the trombones answer it. The tune still travels downwards, but its long phrases have room to sing.
cues.evidence: Queensland Symphony Orchestra, Symphony No. 6 learning resource, p. 17, describes the horns, strings and trombone answer. D-major second theme: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphony_No._6_(Tchaikovsky).
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Bewilderment in Petersburg
cues.text: Tchaikovsky conducts the first performance in Saint Petersburg on 28 October 1893. Two days later he writes to his publisher, Jurgenson: “It’s not that it displeased, but it has caused some bewilderment.” He adds that he is more proud of it than of any of his other works.
cues.evidence: Tchaikovsky to Pyotr Jurgenson, letter 5062, 18/30 October 1893, quoted in Tchaikovsky Research’s account of the first performance, 16/28 October 1893. https://en.tchaikovsky-research.net/pages/Symphony_No._6

cues.title: The scales rush down
cues.text: The broad tune gathers speed and fills the orchestra. Fast downward scales carry its climax; the fall that began as a quiet violin lament now runs through the ensemble.
cues.evidence: Queensland Symphony Orchestra, Symphony No. 6 learning resource, p. 17: the Andante grows in passion and speed, reaching its climax in downward scales. https://qso.com.au/uploads/QSO-Learning-Resource-Breathtaking-Tchaikovsky-1-.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The lament returns
cues.text: The strings bring back the opening B-minor melody. Its falling phrases stretch further as the orchestra takes them up, pressing towards another climax.
cues.evidence: Queensland Symphony Orchestra, Symphony No. 6 learning resource, p. 17, describes the return and expansion of the opening theme. https://qso.com.au/uploads/QSO-Learning-Resource-Breathtaking-Tchaikovsky-1-.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The most sincere of all
cues.text: On 14 August 1893, still scoring, Tchaikovsky tells his nephew Vladimir Davydov that the symphony is “the most sincere of all my creations. I love it as I have never loved any of my other musical offspring.” Davydov is its dedicatee.
cues.evidence: Tchaikovsky to Vladimir Davydov, letter 4998, 2/14 August 1893, quoted in Tchaikovsky Research’s composition history; dedication on the title page of the autograph score. https://en.tchaikovsky-research.net/pages/Symphony_No._6

cues.title: Gong and low brass
cues.text: A single tam-tam stroke marks the withdrawal from the climax. Trombones and tuba sing a quiet chorale after the long hold on F♯, the dominant of B minor.
cues.evidence: Tam-tam, dominant harmony and low-brass chorale: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphony_No._6_(Tchaikovsky). Queensland Symphony Orchestra, Symphony No. 6 learning resource, p. 17, includes the chorale score.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The song in B minor
cues.text: The broad melody returns, now in B minor. Muted strings descend over the double basses’ repeated low B. The tune that opened a window onto D major has reached the symphony’s darkest room.
cues.evidence: The transformed second theme, muted strings and final B-minor resolution are described at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphony_No._6_(Tchaikovsky). Low-B bass pulse: Harlow Robinson, https://www.bso.org/works/tchaikovsky-symphony-no-6.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Nine days later
cues.text: Nine days after the première, at a quarter past three on the morning of 6 November 1893, Tchaikovsky dies of cholera in his brother Modest’s flat in Saint Petersburg. Twenty days after the première, Eduard Nápravník conducts the symphony in a memorial concert.
cues.evidence: Alexander Poznansky’s account of Tchaikovsky’s last illness and death, 25 October/6 November 1893 (Tchaikovsky Research, Tchaikovsky: A Life); the memorial performance under Nápravník in Harlow Robinson’s Boston Symphony programme note. https://en.tchaikovsky-research.net/pages/Tchaikovsky:_A_Life https://www.bso.org/works/tchaikovsky-symphony-no-6

cues.title: Cellos and basses remain
cues.text: The final descent passes into the cellos and double basses. The symphony ends down here, almost out of reach, with B minor still sounding.
cues.evidence: Queensland Symphony Orchestra, Symphony No. 6 learning resource, p. 17, describes the bassoons, cellos and basses at the close, https://qso.com.au/uploads/QSO-Learning-Resource-Breathtaking-Tchaikovsky-1-.pdf. Harlow Robinson describes the thinning close at https://www.bso.org/works/tchaikovsky-symphony-no-6.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: The bassoon leads towards D major
transitions.from: A · A melody between two violins
transitions.how: A descending bassoon line dies away over horns and strings. At the Andante, the horns support a new D-major melody in the first violins and violas. Trombones answer its broad downward sweep.
transitions.evidence: Queensland Symphony Orchestra, Symphony No. 6 learning resource, p. 17; D-major key: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphony_No._6_(Tchaikovsky). https://qso.com.au/uploads/QSO-Learning-Resource-Breathtaking-Tchaikovsky-1-.pdf

transitions.title: The strings reopen the lament
transitions.how: The Andante’s climax breaks into fast descending scales and subsides. The opening string melody returns in B minor, its long falling phrases replacing the rush of notes.
transitions.evidence: Queensland Symphony Orchestra, Symphony No. 6 learning resource, p. 17, describes the downward scales and the return of the opening theme. https://qso.com.au/uploads/QSO-Learning-Resource-Breathtaking-Tchaikovsky-1-.pdf

transitions.title: F♯ fades into the brass chorale
transitions.how: The climax holds F♯ in the bass and gradually loses force. A single tam-tam stroke sounds in the withdrawal; quiet trombones and tuba take over with a chorale. Their chords round off the dominant harmony before the last B-minor return.
transitions.evidence: Dominant pedal, tam-tam and chorale: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphony_No._6_(Tchaikovsky). Chorale score reproduced in Queensland Symphony Orchestra’s learning resource, p. 17.

transitions.title: The broad melody settles into B minor
transitions.to: B′ · The last descent in B minor
transitions.how: After the low-brass chorale, muted strings recover the broad second melody in B minor. Double basses pulse on low B underneath it. The falling phrases pass progressively into the lower strings as the other instruments stop.
transitions.evidence: Second-theme return and final scoring: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphony_No._6_(Tchaikovsky); Harlow Robinson, Boston Symphony programme note, https://www.bso.org/works/tchaikovsky-symphony-no-6.

source.title: Tchaikovsky, Symphony No. 6, Op. 74, miniature score (Leipzig: Ernst Eulenburg, [1928], plate E.E. 3892)
source.locator: IV. Finale, printed pp. 185–208 (bars 1–170); bar numbers placed between the file’s section times

timeline.note: Divided violins trade the falling lament; flutes and bassoons double softly.
Winds swell with the strings to fortissimo, then fall away.
A wind trio and a bassoon line lead out of the lament over soft strings.
D-major Andante: broad string melody, repeated horn notes, clarinet and bassoon.
Pulsing woodwind repeated notes; horns, trumpets and trombones answer in a crescendo.
The climax: full orchestra in fortissimo with timpani; violins in sweeping runs.
After the climax, winds, horns and strings fall back to piano.
The lament returns in the strings, with bassoons and horns.
Stringendo: winds, horns and trumpets drive the strings upward.
Pesante: trombones, tuba and timpani join; marked and heavy in fortissimo.
F♯ held and dying away: winds, horns, low brass and timpani lose force.
A quiet trombone and tuba chorale, with the single tam-tam.
B minor: muted violins and wind chords over the basses’ low pulse.
The winds fall away; a bassoon line over low strings.
Only cellos and basses remain, fading to pianissimo.

composer.epithet: He could make a ballroom glitter, then let one unguarded melody tell us who was unhappy there.
facts: School of Jurisprudence; Saint Petersburg Conservatory, 1862–65, with Anton Rubinstein and Nikolai Zaremba
Nadezhda von Meck: an allowance, 1877–90, and a friendship conducted by letter
Three ballets; Eugene Onegin, The Queen of Spades and other operas
composer.background:
At Kamenka on 6 July 1878, Tchaikovsky was explaining to Nadezhda von Meck how he composed. Ideas arrived in the middle of conversations; he held them in his head until he could sketch them on the first sheet of paper that came to hand. Waiting for the right mood was no way to work. “Inspiration is a guest who does not like to visit the idle,” he told her. Then he broke off for dinner. At two o’clock he resumed, moving on to sketching, orchestration, fair copies and how far a symphony must keep to its traditional form. Here is the composer of extravagant passions in his own voice: observant, companionable, exact about his trade.

He was born in Votkinsk, where his father managed an ironworks. He grew deeply attached to his French governess, Fanny Dürbach, and began piano lessons at the end of 1845. The profession chosen for him was the law. In 1850 he entered the preparatory class of the Imperial School of Jurisprudence in Saint Petersburg. Four years later his mother died of cholera. He graduated in 1859 and took a post at the Ministry of Justice, while opera and concerts increasingly claimed his attention.
